newsitem.title: USA: Slowing housing sector in pace with braking economy.
newsitem.headline: Slowing housing sector in pace with braking economy.

text.p: The housing sector cooled off last month on the heels of a record-setting spring, and economists Monday predicted a more languid pace until year-end, in line with a slowing economy.

Existing home sales fell for a second straight month in July, dropping by 0.5 percent to a 4.14 million annual rate, the National Association of Realtors said. That followed a 2.8 percent decline in June to 4.16 million units.
The July rate was still above the 4.10 million that Wall Street economists had generally forecast.

"It's indicating that the housing market is cooling off, but it's still on balance pretty healthy," said Joseph Carson, chief fixed-income economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "It does play into the view, however, that the economy is slowing," he added.

Carson also noted that July showed the first drop in home prices since February. The NAR report said the median price for existing single-family homes fell to $121,400 in July from $122,900 in June. The median is the midpoint in the price range.

The dip in existing home sales in July was not a source for concern, as the rate was still higher than in any month last year, NAR said. July's pace was up 4.3 percent from the same month in 1995, when it was 3.97 million, NAR said.
The July figure also followed an all-time high in May of a 4.28 million sales rate, the group said.
"Anytime a new record is set in the pace of sales, it's inevitable that some slowdown will follow," said John Tuccillo, NAR chief economist.
Relatively high interest rates also helped curb sales, with the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate at 8.25 percent in July, down from 8.32 percent in June.
That still represents a significant runup in mortgage rates since January, when they averaged 7.03 percent.
The June mortgage rate was the highest average so far this year. The last time the average rate reached that level was in April 1995, NAR said.
NAR President Art Godi said interest rates "are showing signs of leveling off."

Strength in the housing sector earlier this year was partly in response to climbing interest rates, which pushed some homebuyers off the fence and into the market to avoid even higher rates in the future, another economist said.

"I would also add though that interest rates are not altogether that high. Many people would view them as still attractive relative to historical standards, and we have a solid job market in the U.S.," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
"I think housing is not about to collapse. It should be well-maintained, but we are seeing some cooling off from what we saw in the first half of the year," he added.

Economists were mixed over whether the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates before the end of the year, when the economy is expected to slow down from the 3 percent growth rate in the first six months.
The housing sector added about half a percentage point to gross domestic product growth in the first half of the year, and was likely to add nothing in the second half of 1996, Moran said.
Separately, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. released a survey that showed residential and commercial real estate market conditions improved during the three months ended in late July.
The composite index of residential and commercial real estate markets rose to 68 in July from 67 in April. July's reading was the highest since 72 in July 1994, the FDIC said.
A reading above 50 indicates more respondents said conditions were improving than declining. The survey was conducted among 316 mostly bank and thrift examiners at the regulatory agencies.
